**Bottom line.** If isolation of symptomatic cases is 80% effective, cutting the mean delay from onset to isolation from 7 to 5 days would avert about `\pctMedEightyFive{}`{=latex} of the next 12 months' cases and from 7 to 3 days about `\pctMedEightyThree{}`{=latex}, turning a plateau ($\Rt{}\approx\fitBReAfterMed{}$) into decline. Even at 50% effectiveness a 3-day delay averts `\pctMedFiftyThree{}`{=latex}. The effect is large because the outbreak sits at the epidemic threshold, and it reverses if the true current delay is already under 5 days, so the delay must be measured.

# Question and approach {#question-and-approach .unnumbered}

By 12 September 2026 the DRC had `\nConfirmed{}`{=latex} confirmed cases and a modelled incidence of about `\fitBincEndMed{}`{=latex} new cases per day. We asked how many cases would be prevented, and how much sooner transmission would end, if the mean delay from symptom onset to isolation fell from 7 to 5 or 3 days, with isolation that is 50%, 80% or 100% effective (reducing transmission of isolated cases by that fraction). We used a deterministic susceptible--exposed--infectious--isolated--removed (SEIQR) model (Fig. `\ref{fig:model}`{=latex}) with isolation rate $\tau=1/\text{delay}$; isolated people transmit at $1-\epsilon$ of the rate of others, so $\Rt{}=(\beta/\gamma)\{1-\epsilon\,\tau/(\tau+\gamma)\}$ (details in the manuscript appendix). The model was fitted by maximum likelihood to confirmed cases by report date up to 12 September [@bvdoutbreaksize2026], allowing one change in transmission (cross-checked against the onset curve corrected for reporting delay). It fitted well (95% predictive coverage `\fitBcover{}`{=latex}). Transmission grew ($\Rt{}$ `\fitBReBeforeMed{}`{=latex}) until about `\fitBtc{}`{=latex} and has since plateaued ($\Rt{}$ `\fitBReAfter{}`{=latex}).

# Scenarios and uncertainty {#scenarios-and-uncertainty .unnumbered}

Nine scenarios (delay 7, 5, 3 days $\times$ $\epsilon$ 50, 80, 100%) start on 12 September 2026. Each of `\nDraws{}`{=latex} paired draws combines the fitted growth rate and incidence with latent (mean 6.3 d, range 4.0--10.1) and infectious periods (mean 7 d, range 5--10) drawn from triangular distributions [@ebengo2026; @chowell2014]; transmission is calibrated so the 7-day baseline reproduces the fitted growth, and only the delay changes between scenarios. Outcomes: cumulative symptomatic cases over 12 months, cases averted versus the 7-day delay, and months until fewer than one exposed or infectious person remains. We also ran a stochastic version (`\nStoch{}`{=latex} replicates), partial-rank-correlation and `\nVariants{}`{=latex} structural sensitivity analyses, and an out-of-sample forecast check. All code is in R; the repository regenerates every number and figure.

# Results {#results .unnumbered}

```{=latex}

```
With a 7-day delay the model projects `\baseCases{}`{=latex} cases over 12 months and transmission that persists beyond five years. At 80% effectiveness a 5-day delay lowers $\Rt{}$ to `\ReMedEightyFive{}`{=latex} and a 3-day delay to `\ReMedEightyThree{}`{=latex}, with transmission ending after a median of `\durEightyFive{}`{=latex} and `\durEightyThree{}`{=latex} months. At 50% effectiveness the corresponding times are `\durFiftyFive{}`{=latex} and `\durFiftyThree{}`{=latex} months; at 100% they are `\durHundredFive{}`{=latex} and `\durHundredThree{}`{=latex} months. Returns diminish: the first two days saved (7 to 5) avert more than the next two.

# How robust is this? {#how-robust-is-this .unnumbered}

The stochastic model gave the same medians (ratio `\stochRatioMin{}`{=latex}--`\stochRatioMax{}`{=latex}). The isolation delay (partial rank correlation `\prccIsolationDelay{}`{=latex}) and effectiveness (`\prccIsolationEffectiveness{}`{=latex}) dominate the uncertainty, followed by baseline growth (`\prccGrowthRate{}`{=latex}). Across assumptions (natural history, Erlang-distributed delays, delay defined among isolated cases, 90-day roll-out) the 5-day benefit stayed between `\varFiveMin{}`{=latex} and `\varFiveMax{}`{=latex}% and the 3-day benefit between `\varThreeMin{}`{=latex} and `\varThreeMax{}`{=latex}%. **The exception is the baseline delay:** if the true current delay were 4.6 days, a "5-day" target would increase cases (percentage averted: `\varBaseFourFive{}`{=latex}). A forecast using data to 12 September overestimated the next 46 days of cases by `\valErrLong{}`{=latex}, so absolute counts should be read as conditional on the plateau.

# Decision relevance and limits {#decision-relevance-and-limits .unnumbered}

Shortening the delay (community alert networks, decentralised sampling, rapid results, nearby isolation capacity) is worth the most when isolation is also effective; a quick delay with poor isolation helps less. Percent reductions apply while the outbreak is near $\Rt{}\approx1$; at higher $\Rt{}$ a 3-day delay alone suffices only if baseline $\Rt{}\le\critReEightyThree{}$ (80% effectiveness). Limits: the 7-day baseline comes from the project brief and is not confirmed; isolation effectiveness is assumed, not estimated; infectiousness is constant and contact tracing, funerals and spatial structure are omitted; national data are treated as homogeneous.
